data.abstract: Reliable cropland maps are critical for agricultural monitoring, food security, and water resource management. However, global 10-m land cover products, such as European Space Agency (ESA) WorldCover, tend to overestimate cropland in hyperarid regions because irrigated noncropland vegetation (e.g., urban greenery and amenity landscapes) is frequently misclassified as cropland. The objective of this study is to improve the reliability of the ESA WorldCover cropland product in hyperarid environments by developing and evaluating a phenology-guided refinement framework that specifically targets commission errors arising from irrigated noncropland vegetation. Using United Arab Emirates (UAE) as a case study, we derive multitemporal Sentinel-2 vegetation indices and phenological metrics to automatically generate high-confidence annual cropland and irrigated noncropland labels, train a random forest classifier, and apply hysteresis thresholding to produce a refined 10-m resolution cropland map. Validation confirms that the classifier achieves balanced performance at the operational threshold [F1-score = 0.93, overall accuracy (OA) = 0.93, and intersection-over-union (IoU) = 0.87]. Independent evaluation with very-high-resolution (VHR) imagery shows that 90%–97% of pixels removed from the original WorldCover cropland class are correctly identified as noncropland, as captured by the false positive removal accuracy (FPRA) metric. Emirate-level comparison with official statistics indicates that the refinement removes more than 50 km2 of false positives in intensive farming emirates, reducing area-weighted commission error by 78% and lowering estimated irrigation water demand in Abu Dhabi by approximately 24 million m3 per year. The proposed framework provides a robust and transferable approach for refining global cropland products in hyperarid regions, supporting more realistic cropland statistics and water budgeting.

data.title: Earth observation data uncover green spaces’ role in mental health

openAccessPdf.disclaimer: Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11384788, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use.

data.abstract: The prevalence of mental health disorders, a key disability cause, is linked to demographic and socioeconomic factors. However, limited data exists on mental health and the urban environment. Urbanization exposes populations to environmental stressors, particularly affecting low-middle-income countries with complex urban arrangements. We used remote sensing and census data to investigate potential connections between environmental factors and mental health disorders. Land cover variables were assessed using the European Space Agency (ESA) global WorldCover product at 10 m resolution together with the database of mental health diagnosed cases (n = 5769) from the Brazilian Unified Health System’s Department of Informatics (DATASUS) from every health facility of the city of Porto Alegre. The association of mental health data with land cover was established with machine learning algorithms and polynomial regression models. The results suggest that higher trees cover at neighborhood level was associated with better mental health index. A lower mental health index was also found to be associated with an higher Human Development Index. Our results highlight the potential of greenness in the city environment to achieve substantially better mental health outcomes.

data.title: Accuracies, discrepancies, and challenges of the 10 m global land cover products in mountains

data.abstract: ABSTRACT The integration of advanced remote sensing technology, machine learning, and cloud computing platforms has resulted in a new era of high-resolution (10 meter) Global Land Cover (GLC) products. These GLC products often adopt varying methodological frameworks, leading to potentially inconsistent classification outcomes that hinder their usability. This challenge could particularly be more pronounced in mountainous areas because their complex terrain and frequent mountain/cloud shadows make accurate Land Cover (LC) classification difficult. To investigate this issue, we assessed the reliability of three 10-m GLC products: ESRI Land Use/Land Cover, ESA WorldCover, and Dynamic World (DW). We examined their thematic accuracy and spatial and area consistency at the global, continental, and major mountain range levels (24 ranges in total). Our statistical assessment showed that ESRI demonstrated the highest overall accuracy (68.5 ± 0.42%) at the global mountain level, with a small lead over ESA (66.1 ± 0.42%) and DW (65.6 ± 0.45%). However, none of the three GLC products consistently excelled at continental and major mountain levels, underscoring significant regional variability. While water class exhibited F1-scores of more than 85%, other classes (e.g. mixed vegetation and cropland) showed F1-scores of between 40% and 70%. Additionally, we noted substantial discrepancies in the area estimates for key LC classes. Notably, only 53% of pixels had perfect agreement among products at the global scale, with particularly poor consistency across complex terrains such as the Tian Shan and Zagros mountains. Overall, this study provides actionable insights for users of GLC data in global mountainous regions and emphasizes the urgency of addressing classification inconsistencies in future products. To support future research and validation efforts, we provide open access to the dataset of approximately 56,000 validation sample points collected in this study at https://zenodo.org/records/15354081.
